newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: COFFEE-Colombian harvest running behind schedule.
newsitem.headline: COFFEE-Colombian harvest running behind schedule.

text.p: Colombia's main coffee harvest is not only expected to be a poor one but it will come in later than usual this year, industry officials said this week.
The harvest normally begins in mid to late September, but in some areas of the country it is expected to be delayed a full two months because of unusually heavy rains during the flowering period.

"There's going to be a delay in the start of the harvest, we probably won't get started until November," Jesus Chavarro, a senior official of regional Coffee Growers Committee in southwestern Huila province said.
Other growers such as Octavio Jaramillo, who sits on the Coffee Growers Committee in central Caldas province, said delays in the start of the harvest would be limited to no more than about two weeks.
But private exporters said any slowdown, be it weeks or months, comes as bad news in a market already suffering from tight supply.
"I don't know if we're going to be able to meet our October (export) commitments because there's simply no coffee," one exporter told Reuters.
"We'll have to wait and see if the Federation will sell to private exporters, at least until the bulk of the harvest comes to the market," he said.

Foreign Trade Minister Morris Harf said earlier this month that Colombia would be forced to draw on internal stocks maintained by the National Coffee Growers Federation to meet its export commitments this year.

Harf did not elaborate on how much would be sold from the stockpiles, but he spoke a day after a report from the National Planning Department and Finance Ministry said parchment coffee production dropped 5.9 percent during the first half of 1996 and was expected to fall another 5.8 percent by year's end.

Harf said Colombia would export a total of 10.6 million 60- kilo bags of coffee this year, including 5.15 million bags between July and December. Colombia normally retains about one million 60-kilo bags from a given year's crop to meet domestic demand and replenish inventories.
The National Coffee Growers Federation has estimated total production for the 1996 calendar year at 10.5 million bags, down from 12.5 million in 1995.

In addition to foul weather, growers say the 1996 crop has been hurt by soaring production costs, including those associated with fighting the berry borer -- a plague that threatens to ravish trees across the country.
Jaramillo said the upcoming harvest in Caldas would yield about 15 to 20 percent less coffee than last year's and Chavarro in Huila said the crop there was expected to be about 35 percent smaller.
"That's 105,000 loads (125-kilo bags) less than normal," Chavarro said, adding that Huila's average annual production is about 575,000 125-kilo bags.
Contributing to the murky outlook for coffee is a two-week- old offensive by leftist guerrillas across much of Colombia in which scores of soldiers and police have died.

The fighting, some of the worst in more than three decades of guerrilla warfare, has included skirmishes in the central coffee- growing province of Tolima and rebel barricades across roadways or attacks on transport in widespread parts of the country.
"Shipments are going to be kind of risky," one exporter said of getting coffee to port once the harvest finally gets under way.
"The situation is scary and unpredictable," she added, saying the rebel offensive was clearly going "to jeopardize some deliveries" unless it abated in advance of the harvest.
